title: Ya-Sin, heart of the book
hook: often recited for the dying and on Thursday nights in many communities
tomorrow: The man from the city's edge

segments.voice: Yesterday, white, red and black mountains, and your line was knowledge brings awe. What ordinary thing got bigger when you learned about it? Day five hundred forty-eight.

A hospital room, late. A grandmother is very ill, and the family has gathered. Someone opens a small, worn booklet, or a phone, and begins to recite in Arabic, softly, steadily, for about twenty minutes. In a mosque across town, it's Thursday evening, and a circle of people is reciting the same words. In a cemetery, someone stands by a grave and reads it again. Across much of the Muslim world, one surah is the one people reach for at the edges of life. It begins with two letters: Ya. Sin.

Surah thirty-six, eighty-three verses. Its name is its first verse: two Arabic letters, ya and sin, said by themselves. We've met these before, the disconnected letters that open twenty-nine surahs. What they mean, most scholars say, Allah knows best. Some say Ya-Sin is a name for the Prophet ﷺ, and it's become a boy's name in many countries. The text doesn't say. Then, Pickthall: "By the wise Qur'an, Lo! thou art of those sent". An oath on the book itself, and a reassurance to the Prophet that he's a real messenger. So why is it called the heart of the Qur'an? A hadith in the collection of al-Tirmidhi says everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin. Another, in Abu Dawud, says recite Ya-Sin over your dying. Here's the honest part: many hadith scholars grade both reports as weak in their chains. Others accept them, or point to the surah's content. And the content is the key. Ya-Sin is about the things a dying person, and a grieving family, most need to hear: that the messengers were true, that the dead will be raised, that the One who made you the first time can make you again. Its closing verses ask, can't He who created the heavens and the earth create their like? Read at a bedside, that's not abstract theology. It's a promise said aloud in a hard room. So Ya-Sin earned its place in many communities on two grounds: reports that some accept and some question, and a message everyone can hear. Over the next three days, we'll open it.
screen: `A PROMISE SAID IN A HARD ROOM.`

segments.voice: The outline's practice is to listen to Ya-Sin once, and the whole surah takes about twenty minutes, so let today be the beginning. If you can, play the opening of a recitation of Ya-Sin, in Arabic, and simply listen, whether or not you understand the words. Notice the rhythm, how many verses end on the same sound. If you can't play it now, sit and remember someone you've lost, or someone who's ill, and hold them in mind quietly. The bell holds the time.
Ya-Sin. Surah thirty-six, named for its two opening letters, recited for the dying and on Thursday nights in many communities. Today's word.
Your line: the heart of the book. Today, find twenty minutes, on a walk or before sleep, and listen to all of Ya-Sin once. Day five hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: In many Muslim communities Ya-Sin is recited beside the dying, at graves, and on Thursday evenings before Friday; scholars differ on the strength of the hadith behind these customs.
